newsitem.title: UK: Dollar closes lower but well supported in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Dollar closes lower but well supported in Europe.

text.p: The dollar closed lower against the mark and the yen in Europe amid disappointment about its failure to sustain a rally after the U.S. rate rise.

The U.S. currency bounced back, however, from an overnight low at 1.6760 marks amid talk of good buying interest in the 1.6770-50 mark area, traders said. Against the yen, it struggled a touch higher but fresh concern about the politically sensitive U.S.-Japanese trade deficit capped the upside.
Dollar/yen dropped overnight after a comment by U.S. Deputy Treasury Lawrence Summers that his country has expressed concerns about a possible rise in Japan's current account surplus.
The trade deficit will be a market focus next week when Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin visits Tokyo.
At 1608 GMT the dollar was at 1.6766/74 marks and 123.56/53 yen compared with 1.6920/26 and 124.12/17 in late European trading on Wednesday.
But the U.S. unit remained well supported on dips, and thin trade ahead of the Easter weekend exaggerated some of the dollar's movements, traders said.
Key for the direction of dollar/yen will be the investment decisions Japanese players take at the start of Japan's financial year next week, analysts said.
The U.S. rate rise on Tuesday has increased the pull on Japanese cash as prospects for higher rates in Japan remain dim.

"As long as the markets retain a bullish interpretation of what the Fed has been doing, then the U.S. will continue to attract Japanese money," said Roger Francis, senior analyst at IJB International.
A flow of funds out of Japan is likely to put pressure on the yen and would put the 125 yen level back into focus.
"If Japanese investors resume their buying of high-yielding currencies the yen is going to weaken aginst most major currencies," said Brian Martin, chief economist forex at BZW.
A spate of U.S. data had scant impact on the dollar. Weekly jobless claims fell to 310,000 from a revised 314,000 the previous week and against 313,000 forecast.
Existing home sales rose 9.0 percent in February to 4.26 million uits from 3.91 million in January and versus 4.1 million expected.
The University of Michigan final index of consumer sentiment rose to 100.0 in March from 99.7 in February and 101.3 forecast.
Elsewhere, the lira rallied against the mark after the Italian cabinet approved its corrective mini-budget as expected.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi said the budget will help Italy to meet the Maastricht criteria.
Mark/lira was at 998.30/80 versus 999.20/50 just before the budget approval and 996.50/80 late on Wednesday.
